entries.title: Understanding comes before talking
entries.body: Many children around the first birthday follow simple words and directions well before they say many words themselves. The AAP counts pointing, gestures, and sounds as real communication at this age. Describe what you are doing together through the day, and put phones and the TV away during these talks. Your pediatrician can answer speech questions at the next check-up.

entries.title: Picky eating is common at this age
entries.body: The AAP calls picky eating common in toddlers, and it says a child may need many tastes before accepting a new food. Offering a refused food again, without pressure, tends to work better than pushing. CDC lists feeding themselves with their fingers among the skills many children show by 15 months. Eat the same meal together when you can, and agree between you not to use sweets as a reward. Ask your pediatrician if mealtimes worry you.

entries.title: What goes in the cup
entries.body: The AAP names water and plain milk as the best drinks for young children, and suggests skipping sugary drinks and flavored milk. CDC's 15-month page also mentions practicing with an open cup. Decide together what is offered at home, at grandparents', and in the car, so the answer is the same from both of you. Your pediatrician can tell you how much milk and juice fit your child.

entries.title: Tantrums are a normal part of growing
entries.body: Tantrums are a normal part of development and are most common between ages 1 and 3. Hunger and tiredness often set them off, so a snack and a steady nap plan can help. During one, a choice between two options or a change of scene may redirect your child. Hitting and biting still need a calm, firm stop. CDC lists checking that you are nearby among the things many children do now.

entries.title: A simple bedtime routine
entries.body: For toddlers who resist bedtime, consider a calm wind-down such as a book or soft music, at about the same time each night. Its sleep guidance counts naps toward the daily total and says needs differ from child to child. Keep wake-up times similar on weekends. Take turns leading the routine so your child is comfortable with either of you, and mention ongoing sleep trouble to your pediatrician.

entries.title: Reading together every day
entries.body: CDC lists looking at a few pages of a book with you among the things many children do by 18 months. Its tips for ages 1 to 2 suggest reading daily and answering a first word with the full one, so "baba" becomes "bottle". Choose sturdy picture books, let your child turn the pages, and let each of you read at a different time of day so books are not only one parent's job.

entries.title: Safety for a child who runs and climbs
entries.body: Many children heading toward age 2 run and walk up a few stairs, CDC notes, so it is a good time to look at safety again. Consider staying within arm's reach near any water, using stair gates, keeping medicines and cleaners capped and out of sight, and keeping the car seat rear-facing up to its limit. Save the Poison Help number, 1-800-222-1222, in both your phones.

entries.title: Screens and a toddler's day
entries.body: Consider against TV and apps before 18 months apart from video calls, because young children learn best from people and hands-on play. A TV left on in the background can also mean fewer words spoken to a toddler. Decide together what screens look like at home, including your own phones, and watch alongside your child when they do watch. Your pediatrician can help with a plan.

entries.title: House rules you both enforce
entries.body: Children learn by watching adults and respond to warm attention for behavior you like. Agree on two or three simple rules, such as no hitting and staying close near the street, and answer the same way each time. Praise specific effort, like listening the first time. Unsafe behavior always needs a response. CDC lists noticing when others are upset among the skills around age 2.

entries.title: Signs of toilet learning readiness
entries.body: There is no fixed start date for toilet learning. A child needs to notice the urge, understand what it means, and be able to tell you they need help, and that waiting until your child is truly ready tends to make it faster and more pleasant. Watch for those signs together, and agree on how you will each respond to accidents. Ask your pediatrician if you are unsure.

entries.title: Two words at a time
entries.body: CDC lists saying at least two words together, pointing to body parts, and using gestures such as nodding yes among the things many children do by age 2. Language varies widely at this age, and a quieter child may know as many words as a chatty one. Read short books where your child can point and name things. If you have worries, your pediatrician can check hearing and talk through next steps.

entries.title: Sharing the hard moments
entries.body: Toddlers feel big feelings, and so do their parents. The AAP tantrum tips suggest handing over to another caregiver when your frustration rises, and keeping your responses consistent from day to day. Agree on a small signal that means "tag me in", and make sure each of you gets a short break this week. CDC notes many children look at your face to see how to react, so your calm helps.

entries.title: Playing next to other children
entries.body: Playing alongside other children, and sometimes with them, is on CDC's list for around 30 months. The AAP describes preschoolers moving from side-by-side play to playing together, with sharing growing through practice. Short playdates with one or two children and a parent nearby give your child practice. Name turns out loud when they happen, and take turns yourselves at home.

entries.title: Pretend play takes off
entries.body: Pretend play appears on CDC's list for 30 months, along with solving small problems like pulling over a stool to reach something. Its tips for ages 2 to 3 suggest pretend play and games like follow-the-leader. Feed a doll, run a toy shop, or make a bus from chairs. Let your child lead the story, and take turns being the customer or the patient.

entries.title: Moving, jumping, climbing
entries.body: Jumping off the ground with both feet is on CDC's list for around 30 months. For younger children active play is the best exercise, and CDC's tips for ages 2 to 3 suggest free active play plus walks or wagon rides. Pick one active outing each of you does with your child every week, such as the park or a dance break in the living room.

entries.title: Supervision is the main safety tool
entries.body: Children from 2 to 4 do not yet understand danger or reliably obey "no", so close supervision matters most. It suggests keeping your child away from the stove while you cook, testing smoke alarms monthly, using a harnessed car seat in the back, and asking about firearm storage in homes your child visits. Your pediatrician can answer injury prevention questions.

entries.title: A family plan for screens
entries.body: The AAP's guide for ages 2 to 4 suggests looking at your child, the content, calm, what screens crowd out, and how you talk about what they watch. It advises against using a device to soothe an upset or bored child. Write a short family plan together, including your own phone habits, so play, outdoor time, reading, and talking keep their place. Your pediatrician can help adjust it.

entries.title: Small routines and small jobs
entries.body: Following simple daily routines when asked, and two-step directions, are on CDC's list for around 30 months. Consider simple household tasks and step-by-step reminders for dressing, and notes that praising effort builds confidence. Choose one routine, such as shoes by the door after a walk, and use the same words each time. Praise the trying, not only the result.

entries.title: Getting ready for preschool
entries.body: Around age 3, CDC lists calming down within about ten minutes after a caregiver leaves and joining other children to play. If preschool or childcare is coming, consider asking providers about their food and screen-time policies. Visit together, practice short goodbyes with a trusted adult, and agree who does drop-off. Ask your pediatrician how your child is doing.

entries.title: Why, why, why
entries.body: CDC lists holding back-and-forth conversations and asking who, what, where, and why questions among the things many children do by age 3. The AAP notes that speech is often about three-quarters understandable to strangers around 3 to 4. Answer the questions, even repeated ones, and ask what your child thinks. Mention any speech worries at the next check-up.

entries.title: Bad dreams and night fears
entries.body: Nightmares are most common between ages 3 and 12, while night terrors are most common in toddlers and preschoolers. After a nightmare, comfort your child quickly and remind them it was not real. During a night terror a child may seem unresponsive and will not remember it, so stay calm and keep them safe. Agree who goes in at night, and talk to your pediatrician if episodes continue.

entries.title: Imagination and imaginary friends
entries.body: The AAP describes fantasy play as a healthy outlet, and says imaginary friends are usually a sign of creativity rather than loneliness. Three-year-olds can have trouble telling pretend from real, and scary stories can feel true to them. Comfort a frightened child without teasing. Join their play now and then, and let your child steer the story. The AAP adds that by age 4 most children separate fantasy from reality more easily.

entries.title: Taking turns and saying sorry
entries.body: Preschoolers learn to take turns in small groups, and it suggests teaching words for feelings and wants, such as "use your words". Calmly stopping hitting while acknowledging the feeling works better than shouting, and apologies mean more once a child understands what happened. CDC lists noticing other children and joining their play at this age. Show turn-taking and calm problem solving yourselves.

entries.title: Body names and privacy
entries.body: Consider teaching the proper names for body parts and explaining that areas covered by a swimsuit, and the mouth, are private. It also suggests asking before hugs and respecting a child's no, offering a wave or high five instead. Use everyday moments like bath time, and answer questions calmly and briefly. Both of you can use the same words. Ask your pediatrician for more guidance.

entries.title: Making books part of bedtime
entries.body: CDC lists saying words from a song, story, or rhyme and telling what comes next in a familiar story among the things many children do by age 4. Consider a bedtime book habit of around 20 to 30 minutes with the TV off, and asking your child to describe the pictures. Take turns choosing the book, and try the library story hour together.

entries.title: Getting ready for kindergarten
entries.body: Kindergarten readiness is more than letters and numbers. Taking turns, listening, managing feelings, and making friends count just as much, and children develop at different rates. CDC lists following rules in games and telling a story with two events at age 5. Ask your pediatrician and your child's preschool teacher what they see, and talk about the school day together.

entries.title: Safety on bikes, streets, and water
entries.body: Five-year-olds are learning risky skills but cannot yet judge what is safe, so adults still need to supervise. It suggests a helmet on every bike ride, stopping at the curb, swim lessons with an adult always nearby, a booster seat until the belt fits, and locked firearm storage. Save emergency numbers in both phones, and consider learning first aid and CPR.

entries.title: Chores and a sense of responsibility
entries.body: Consider asking children of this age to help with household tasks such as setting the table, and notes that doing simple chores is on its list for age 5. Handing over tasks shows trust and builds confidence, and that mistakes are part of learning. Share a short job list between you and the child, and praise effort rather than only results.

entries.title: A homework routine that works
entries.body: Consider a well-lit homework spot with supplies, a regular time such as after an afternoon snack, and doing your own work nearby while your child does theirs. It also describes a bedtime that leaves enough sleep. Consider meeting the teachers and continuing to read together, taking turns as reading grows. Agree which of you handles which evening.

entries.title: Friends matter more now
entries.body: Friendships and being accepted become more important in middle childhood, and that children may face peer pressure as they get older. It suggests talking about friends, meeting their families, and joining teams or groups. If your child feels left out, consider acknowledging how hard that is first, then talking with the teacher if it keeps happening. Your pediatrician can help too.
